notes:
I've drafted notes for most verses below. A few gaps up front:

- **Sources I couldn't reach:** I didn't get to any Catholic or Orthodox site pages (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), any Lutheran site, or any page on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching about this chapter. The only Catholic material is Haydock's commentary as reproduced on StudyLight, plus a Catholic Bible translation.
- **Verse numbers:** The Hebrew Bible counts v. 1 as 28:69, so every later verse is one number lower there (see v. 1).
- **Thin verses:** I found little on vv. 3, 8, 11 and 13 on their own.

---

**v. 1**
- *Traditional reading:* Guzik says this restates and reaffirms the covenant Israel made at Horeb about 40 years earlier. Most of the people who had the covenant blood sprinkled on them had died in the wilderness, so the covenant had to be renewed with the generation that would conquer Canaan. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- Matthew Henry: the covenant was the same, but this was a new announcement and ratification of it. He adds that ministers have no power to set the terms of the covenant; they only hand out its seals. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm
- *Where traditions differ:* Precept Austin sets out three views:
  - Most commentators read it as a renewal of the Sinai covenant. Wiersbe argues that a separate covenant would have needed its own blood sacrifices, as at Sinai.
  - Some dispensationalists (J. Vernon McGee, the Scofield Bible) call chapters 29–30 the "Palestinian covenant."
  - MacArthur sees a distinct covenant pointing ahead to the New Covenant, because the focus is on Israel's changed heart (compare 29:4 with 30:6).
  - Jack Deere, of Dallas Seminary (usually counted dispensational), still reads it as a renewal.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary
- *Modern scholarship:* Precept Austin quotes the NET Bible note: the Hebrew text counts this verse as 28:69, so the English and Hebrew numbers differ by one through 29:29. Deere and Currid think this verse closes the ceremony in chapter 28 rather than opening a new speech. — same URL

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik lists what they saw: the plagues, the death of the firstborn, the parted Red Sea, the destroyed Egyptian army, the manna and water, miracle after miracle. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- Utley (bible.org) points to the wordplay: v. 2 says "you have seen," and v. 4 says they cannot see. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29
- Ellicott: the "you" is emphatic — they themselves are the witnesses. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/29.htm

**v. 4** (where the traditions differ most)
- *Shared reading:* They saw the outward events but missed what they meant. The Pulpit Commentary says they saw, and yet did not see: they saw the event but not its inner meaning. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-29.html. Utley notes that Paul and Acts later use this phrase for spiritual blindness (Isa. 6:9–10; Acts 28:26–27; Rom. 11:8). — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29
- *Reformed and Calvinistic Baptist:*
  - Gill (Baptist): an understanding heart, seeing eyes and hearing ears are special gifts of God's grace, given to some and not to others. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-4.html
  - The Geneva Study Bible: people cannot understand God's mysteries unless it is given to them from above. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-4.htm
  - John Piper: if you don't see God as your greatest treasure, one decisive reason is that God has not given you that sight. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant
  - Calvin, quoted by Keil & Delitzsch: by scolding their past dullness, Moses wants to stir them to want understanding now. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-4.htm
  - Robert South (Anglican), quoted in the Biblical Illustrator: the verse refutes the view that simply presenting the truth is enough grace, without a new, powerful work of the Spirit on the heart. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/deuteronomy-29.html
- *Wesleyan and Methodist:*
  - Adam Clarke reports that some scholars read the verse as a question ("Has not God given you a heart?"). Their reason is that God could not blame people for failing a duty when he had given them neither the understanding to see it nor the strength to do it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-4.html
  - Benson: God would have given that heart had they sincerely asked, so they have no excuse. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-4.htm
- *Middle readings:*
  - Matthew Henry: the verse does not put the blame on God, as if they had begged for grace and been refused; it puts the guilt on them. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-4.html
  - Barnes: understanding God's things is God's gift, yet a person who lacks it is not guiltless. Keil & Delitzsch: God had not yet given it because the people had not asked, since they didn't feel the need. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-4.htm
  - Spurgeon (Baptist, in Guzik) gives three reasons for the blindness: they didn't recognise it, never asked God for sight, and resisted the light they had. Guzik (Calvary Chapel; Enduring Word is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list) also warns that miracles alone change no one without the Spirit's work. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: clothes lasting 40 years, feeding a whole nation in the desert, and slaves defeating kingdoms all need a miracle. He then draws spiritual parallels: clothing (Rev. 3:18), shoes (Eph. 6:15), bread and wine (1 Cor. 11). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- Utley: vv. 5–6 show God's care through the whole wilderness period, which was itself a time of judgment. Israel was to look to his provision, not to food and drink made by human hands. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29
- Matthew Henry: God gives food, clothing and wealth to many to whom he does not give grace; many enjoy the gifts without a heart to see the Giver. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik quotes Merrill: the conquest happened only because God the Warrior led them; Israel's history was a record of miracle from start to finish. Guzik applies this to Christians taking ground from spiritual enemies (2 Cor. 10:4–5). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/

**v. 9**
- Guzik: after such great works there is one logical response; knowing God's love and power should have made Israel more committed than ever. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- *Prosperity reading:* I found no source in my results that uses "that you may prosper" this way, so I can't describe that view.

**vv. 10–11**
- Guzik: the covenant took in leaders, men, women, children, servants and foreigners who had joined Israel. Mainly, though not only, by ethnicity, this was a national covenant. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: no one was exempt, in case anyone sliding into idolatry became a "root of bitterness" (Heb. 12:15). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-28.htm

**vv. 12–13**
- *Cutting a covenant:* Guzik says "make" a covenant is literally "cut," recalling the ritual of passing between halved animals (Gen. 15). Clarke reads "enter into" as passing between the parts of the sacrifice. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- *The oath:* Thompson, quoted by Guzik, says the word "oath" here means "curse." Someone who enters a covenant puts themselves where its curses will fall if they break it. — same URL
- *Not a way of salvation:* Guzik: this covenant did not make individuals righteous; that came by faith (Gen. 15:6). — same URL
- Utley: this is a covenant renewal text. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29

**vv. 14–15**
- Thompson, quoted by Guzik: the covenant demand reaches those not yet born; future generations were one with the Israel that swore at Sinai. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/deuteronomy/deuteronomy-29.cfm
- Matthew Henry also applies it to Israelites kept at home by illness or work: they were still bound. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm
- Wiersbe (in Precept Austin) compares later generations being bound by Magna Carta or the US Constitution. He holds the covenant stood until Christ's death (Col. 2:14; Heb. 8:13). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary

**vv. 16–17**
- Precept Austin: on the journey Israel had seen the shrines and idols of the peoples they passed. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary
- Matthew Henry: the main reason for renewing the covenant now was to guard them against idolatry, the sin most likely to ruin them. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm

**v. 18**
- Thompson, quoted by Guzik, pictures idolatry as a plant that roots and yields poison weeds and wormwood. Guzik ties the "root" to compromise and resentment of God's jealousy. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- Utley: the warning is aimed at each individual, family and tribe; the poison is disobedience. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29
- *New Testament use:* The International Critical Commentary on Hebrews notes that Heb. 12:15 echoes this verse in its Greek form. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/hebrews/12-1.html

**v. 19**
- *False peace:* Guzik calls it the peace of the blind, like passengers calm just before a bomb explodes. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/. Barnes says this is the secret, presumptuous sinner who thinks all is well because he prospers. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-19.htm. Utley: this is the typical attitude of sinners who take God's patience as an excuse to keep rebelling. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29
- *The hard phrase* (KJV "to add drunkenness to thirst"; BSB "watered land as well as the dry") is read several ways:
  - Calvin (Reformed): a proverb against stoking fleshly appetites that are already inflamed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-19.html
  - Wesley (Methodist): it may mean "add thirst to drunkenness," that is, piling up sins yet still craving more. — same URL
  - Clarke (Methodist): giving in to every sensual pleasure. Gill (Baptist): drinking idolatry until drunk on it (Rev. 17:2). — same URL
  - Pulpit Commentary, on the Hebrew words: the verb is now generally taken to mean pouring out or destroying, not "add". It prefers "destroy the well-watered land with the dry," meaning that such hardness would destroy everyone. Modern translations like the BSB follow this. — same URL
  - Haydock (Catholic): it may echo "evil company corrupts good morals" — those already "drunk" with sin drag down the "thirsty." He reports that the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads it as keeping the innocent from being caught up in the sinner's ruin. — same URL
  - Ellicott: the sinner thinks one idolater won't ruin the whole nation, and Hebrews answers that "many be defiled." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-19.htm

**v. 20**
- Grisanti, in Precept Austin, lists five strong statements of the coming judgment. The curses are mainly those of chapter 28. Precept Austin links the "blotted out" name to the book of life (Rev. 20). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary
- Guzik: Christ is the one God "did not spare," as substitute for believers (2 Cor. 5:21). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/
- *A real interpretive debate:* Utley calls "never willing to forgive" a hyperbole, to be read against God's readiness to forgive anyone who repents. He mentions people who see a limit to God's grace and says: "I do not accept this." The problem is not God's forgiveness but rebellious people's continual sin; the break comes from the human side. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29

**v. 21**
- Guzik: punishing the covenant-breaker also serves as a lesson for all Israel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-29/

**vv. 22–23**
- Barnes: the picture comes from the Dead Sea area, once fertile until God's judgment (Gen. 13:10; 19:24–25). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-28.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (19th century) sees the barren Palestine of their own day, seen by travellers from Europe, America and the Indies, as fulfilment of this verse. — same URL
- Utley: the land would become like the Dead Sea region where Sodom and Gomorrah stood. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29

**v. 24**
- Utley: Israel was a sign to the nations, meant for blessing but a sign even in judgment. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29
- Matthew Henry: the stress falls on "this land," the good and holy land; judgment begins at the house of God (1 Pet. 4:17). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm

**vv. 25–26**
- Matthew Henry: God never forsakes anyone until they first forsake him. The other gods were ones Israel owed nothing to; God made creatures to serve us, not to be served. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm
- Precept Austin applies this to modern substitutes for God as well as literal idols. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary

**v. 27**
- Utley: Israel's sin affects the land itself. — https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-29

**v. 28**
- Precept Austin: "anger… fury… great wrath" stacked together show that exile would be severe judgment, not light discipline. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary
- Gill applies it to both the Babylonian exile and the Roman scattering, and mentions the oversized letter in the Hebrew text that Jewish commentators linked to the ten lost tribes. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/29-28.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the law leaves sinners uprooted, but Christ's grace plants repentant believers again. — same URL
- Precept Austin (citing Ryrie): God also promised to bring them back (30:1–3), so the outcome finally rests on God's faithfulness. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-29-commentary

**v. 29**
- *Traditional reading:*
  - Pulpit Commentary: the "secret things" are not hidden sins, as one ancient Jewish paraphrase (the Targum) took it, but things in God's purpose known only to him, which may be left with him. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-29.html
  - Barnes: when and how the blessings and curses arrive is God's business; his revealed will is ours to carry out. — same URL
  - Constable: in context it means specifically how Israel would respond to the covenant in the future. — same URL
  - Ellicott: the connection to what comes before is unclear. He cites a Jewish reading that hidden sins are God's to punish, while open ones are the community's to remove. He thinks there is a prophetic note too. — https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/29-29.htm
- *Reformed:* R.C. Sproul ties this to God's hidden or "decretive" will, which ordains everything, and his revealed or "preceptive" will, his commands. He quotes Calvin: where God closes his mouth, I stop asking. — https://www.ligonier.org/posts/secret-things-lord. Ligonier also teaches that this distinction can bring peace when seeking guidance. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-will-hidden-and-revealed
- *Wesleyan:* Benson (Methodist): God's counsels about people and nations, and the timing of his judgments and mercies, are not for us to pry into. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-29.html
- *Contrast on predestination:* One unnamed sermon in the Biblical Illustrator counts "absolute predestination" among the secret matters people have puzzled over to no purpose. Other entries there build the secret-will versus revealed-will distinction. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-29.html
- *A different sentence division:* Matthew Henry and Gill mention a reading that makes it one sentence: "the secret things of the Lord are revealed to us." — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_029.cfm. A Catholic translation, the Catholic Public Domain Version, renders it that way: "These hidden things of the Lord our God have been revealed to us and to our sons…" — https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/29-29.htm
- *Application:*
  - Gill: revelation exists to be practised; hearing and reading are useless unless practised. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/29-29.html
  - GotQuestions: "why" a tragedy happens may be one of the secret things. — https://www.gotquestions.org/secret-things-belong-to-the-Lord.html
  - Utley: people are responsible for the light they have, whether from nature, conscience or Scripture. — https://bible.org/book/export/html/20904
